en: [Siddham] Homage to the Buddha.

Having honored in every way the Fully Awakened One, the Dharma, and the Noble Saṅgha— who have attained the preeminence among the multitudes of beings' qualities through the attainment of purity of intellect and tranquility—
this is a compendium of the True Dharmas established in the Abhidharma.
Because for others [the sense bases] such as the sense-fields (āyatana) and so forth will be established.
The six—eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind—are twofold;
they are internal because they serve as the support for the mind, and they are distinct from a self (ātman).
Visible form, sound, odor, taste, the tangible, and mental phenomena are the objects;
they are external because they are common [to all], and among them, visible form and mental phenomena are primary.
Here, the eye is the observation of visible form, while the ear and the others follow in due order.
These three—mind, speech, and body—are equal when they are inhabited by consciousness.
Form is the object of the eye; sound and the others correspond to their respective sense organs;
and for the mind alone, everything is its object, excluding its own constituent parts.

Form is of twenty kinds, sound is of three, and smell is of six; taste is sevenfold here, the tangible is eightfold, while some say it consists of eleven. Those factors that are formless, excluding the mind, constitute the sphere of mental objects (dharmāyatana); otherwise, they are categorized differently.
Or else, the person is inexpressible, and everything else is otherwise.
That which projects and that which produces is the cause;
that which is about to perish and is immediately preceding serves as the non-obstructing condition.
The intended object of focus is that based upon which [the mind] arises;

however, all other factors exercise sovereignty over the produced [mind] with respect to its obstacles. Arising—whether prior or simultaneous—is the activator even in the case of a dissimilar [moment].
The homogeneous cause (sabhāgahetu) is that which has arisen previously and is similar in its element (bhūmi), category (nikāya), or both.

The pervasive (sarvatraga), associated (saṃprayukta), retributive (vipāka), and co-existent (sahabhū) causes are likewise. The pervasive [causes] pertain to two kinds of subsequent occurrences within their own realm (sadhātukā).

Wherever those which are associated all mutually ripen, for that reason it is called "cooking" (*pakti*); thus another [factor] is its co-arising fruit (*sahabhū-phala*). That which, in fact, becomes the provider of a basis for whatever is being born—

That [unmanifest action] is the immediate [result] for that person; it is the mind and mental factors, and it is the mind. This [unmanifest action] is the object of the associated [factors] in two ways:
some maintain it is only the objects of the associated [factors], while others maintain it is the entirety of them.

The outflow (niṣyanda) is similar to its cause; the ripening (vipāka), it is said, arises from karma. That which is designated as a sentient being is neutral (avyākṛta), though some say it is born through power. The fruit of sovereignty (ādhipatyaphala) is of two kinds, obtained by way of non-obstruction.
Abandonment is dissociation [from defilements] through wisdom; in some cases, it is the fruit of attainment.
Of two [types of karma], there is outflow; of one, there is ripening; of two, there is the fruit of human effort.
However, sovereignty belongs to all [three]; abandonment is the path to liberation.
In two time periods there are two [types of causes], while the others among the three are causes; these [latter] grant their fruit.
Two are present, and the remaining ones are broken; those other than the active [cause] are also broken.
However, it is said that all present [causes] indeed grasp their fruit.
Those belonging to two or one time period perform the function for those that are arising and those that have arisen. (dha) 20 There is also an inclusion here of other causes and fruits;
this very [inclusion] is the benefit, the quality, or else the disadvantage. 21

For among the elements (bhūta), their derivatives (bhautika), consciousness (vijñāna), and mental factors (dharma), there is a mutual production of four, three, two, or one; and here, that [production] of its own genus is of one kind. The elements—earth, water, fire, and air—are so called because of their similarity to the primary elements.
Those characterized by functions such as steadfastness (dhṛti) and hardness (kaṭhinatva), or those that exist simultaneously;
form, sound, mind, and mental objects—these five are of indeterminate nature (avyākṛta).
All of these exist in the realm of desire (kāmadhātu); ten exist in the realm of form (rūpadhātu); and the final two exist in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu).

Furthermore, the mental factors (*caitta*) associated with the untainted (*anāsrava*), such as the *dharmas* beginning with the analytical knowledges (*vidā*), as well as those that are conjoined (*saṃprayukta*) and those that follow along (*anuparivartin*), are all co-existent (*sahabhū*). However, two minds do not exist simultaneously. 25.
Ten [elements] are material; one (sound) alone arises from informative action among the three [realms].
The mind has an object; for three [realms], three [elements] constitute action.
Two are fruition; the others, excluding sound, are produced by effort. || 26–27 ||
Nine are to be cultivated because they arise from the qualities of protection;
all are to be fully understood, while six are to be realized directly.
Ten and a portion of two are to be abandoned by means of the Path.
All [objects] are to be fully known because they are associated with outflows and because they are like suffering.
Or rather, visible forms and sounds are acquired by five [faculties], while the mind and mental objects are of six kinds.
Since this is not the intended meaning, the other eight [categories] are to be abandoned through cultivation.
Initial application (vitarka) and sustained application (vicāra) exist in the desire realm and in the dhyāna born of seclusion;
however, in the intermediate dhyāna (dhyānāntara), there is only sustained application, and beyond that, both are absent.
Joy (prīti) is said to extend up to the second dhyāna, and the arising of bliss (sukha) up to the third.

Because joy has been suppressed, it is said that there are two other [stages] in between. Through the application [of meditation], the production of neither-painful-nor-pleasant [feeling] occurs up to the peak of existence. Due to the excellence of the attenuation of perception, there are four formless stages.
The teaching of [states] such as "with vitarka" is to be understood as occurring either by way of possibility (*saṃbhava*) or by way of association (*saṃprayoga*).
It should be known that in the [meditative] stages (*bhūmi*), it is by way of possibility; whereas in the case of associated [mental factors], it is otherwise.
The first chapter, the Compendium of Bases (*āyatanasamuccaya*), in the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*, is completed.
